subtopic_detail: Adolescent knee pain with obligate external rotation on hip flexion and the weight bearing decision
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 12-year-old boy who has had a dull ache in his left knee for about seven weeks. His mother says he has been walking 'with his foot turned out' and no longer plays soccer at lunchtime.

He recalls no injury. The pain is worse after activity and settles with rest. He has not been febrile and has not been unwell in any other way. His weight is above the 97th centile and his height is on the 25th centile.

On examination the left knee is not warm, has no effusion and moves through a full painless range. The tibial tuberosity is not tender. When you flex the left hip the thigh rolls into external rotation and you cannot flex it in the neutral plane, and internal rotation of the left hip is limited to 10 degrees compared with 40 degrees on the right.

data_table.Knee examination: No effusion, no warmth, full painless range of movement, tibial tuberosity not tender
data_table.Hip examination: Obligate external rotation of the left thigh on hip flexion; left internal rotation 10 degrees, right 40 degrees
data_table.Growth: Weight above the 97th centile, height on the 25th centile

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange knee radiographs and refer to physiotherapy for quadriceps strengthening
options.rationale: Imaging the knee answers the wrong question, because the knee examination is entirely normal and the pain is referred along the obturator nerve from the hip. Loading the joint through a strengthening program before the hip is imaged risks converting a stable slip into an unstable one. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute hip pain and limp)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Acute hip pain and limp

options.text: Advise activity modification with simple analgesia and review him again in six weeks
options.rationale: Activity modification is the treatment for Osgood-Schlatter disease, which produces tenderness localised to the tibial tuberosity that is absent here. A six week delay in a slipped upper femoral epiphysis substantially increases the risk of slip progression and avascular necrosis. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute hip pain and limp)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Acute hip pain and limp

options.text: Keep him non-weight bearing and arrange urgent orthopaedic review with pelvic films
options.rationale: Obligate external rotation on hip flexion with restricted internal rotation in an overweight adolescent is the classic sign of a slipped upper femoral epiphysis, which needs anteroposterior and frog-leg lateral pelvic radiographs and surgical fixation. Non-weight bearing from the moment of suspicion is the intervention that protects the epiphyseal blood supply while transfer is arranged. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute hip pain and limp)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Acute hip pain and limp

options.text: Arrange an urgent knee ultrasound and aspirate any joint effusion that is identified
options.rationale: Aspiration is the right move for a suspected septic joint, which presents with fever, an effusion and pain through a restricted arc, none of which is present over a seven week history. Ultrasound of a clinically normal knee will not identify the proximal femoral pathology. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute hip pain and limp)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Acute hip pain and limp

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the knee and review him once the report arrives
options.rationale: Magnetic resonance imaging of the knee would be reasonable for mechanical knee symptoms such as locking or giving way with a normal radiograph, but the knee here is normal on examination. The delay inherent in outpatient magnetic resonance imaging is also unacceptable when the hip is the problem. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute hip pain and limp)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Acute hip pain and limp

explanation.summary: A slipped upper femoral epiphysis is the commonest hip disorder of adolescence and is missed most often because roughly a quarter of children present with knee or distal thigh pain and no hip complaint at all. The peak age is 10 to 16 years, obesity is the dominant risk factor, and bilateral disease eventually occurs in about a fifth of cases. The single most useful bedside sign is obligate external rotation: as the hip is flexed the thigh rotates outward because the metaphysis has displaced anteriorly relative to the epiphysis. Radiographs must include a frog-leg lateral view, since an early slip can look normal on the anteroposterior film alone. Management is in situ screw fixation, and the key determinant of outcome is whether the slip remains stable, so any child with a suspected slip is made non-weight bearing immediately.
key_points: Examine the hip in every adolescent presenting with knee pain and a normal knee
Obligate external rotation on hip flexion with loss of internal rotation is the hallmark sign
Order anteroposterior and frog-leg lateral pelvic radiographs, not knee films
Make the child non-weight bearing from the moment the diagnosis is suspected
Obesity is the leading risk factor and about 20 per cent eventually slip on the other side
explanation.pearls: On the anteroposterior pelvis, Klein's line drawn along the superior femoral neck should intersect part of the epiphysis; if it passes entirely above the epiphysis the slip is present even when the femoral head still looks round.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Acute hip pain and limp
Australian Orthopaedic Association: Paediatric hip conditions
BMJ Best Practice: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis

subtopic_detail: Frequency of slit lamp screening in antinuclear antibody positive oligoarticular juvenile arthritis
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in a rheumatology clinic. A 3-year-old girl has had a swollen, warm left knee for four months and a swollen right ankle for six weeks. Her mother says she is stiff and clingy in the mornings and loosens up by mid-morning, and that she has not been febrile at any point.

There is no rash and no lymphadenopathy. Both eyes look white and quiet and she has never complained that they hurt or that light bothers her, and she does not rub them.

Investigations show an antinuclear antibody titre of 1:320 with a negative rheumatoid factor. Inflammatory markers are mildly raised. A diagnosis of oligoarticular juvenile idiopathic arthritis is made and intra-articular corticosteroid injection is planned.

data_table.Joints: Left knee and right ankle swollen and warm; morning stiffness easing by mid-morning
data_table.Eyes: White and quiet on external inspection; no pain, photophobia or eye rubbing reported
data_table.Investigations: Antinuclear antibody 1:320, rheumatoid factor negative, C-reactive protein 18 mg/L (less than 5), erythrocyte sedimentation rate 34 mm/h (less than 15)
data_table.Systemic features: No fever, no rash, no lymphadenopathy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate ophthalmic surveillance plan?

options.text: Arrange ophthalmology review only if she develops a red or a painful eye
options.rationale: The uveitis of oligoarticular juvenile idiopathic arthritis is characteristically chronic, anterior and completely asymptomatic, so waiting for a red or sore eye means waiting for a complication. Symptom-triggered review is appropriate in the acute anterior uveitis of an older human leucocyte antigen B27 positive child, which is painful and photophobic. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis)
source_refs: Australian Rheumatology Association: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis

options.text: Arrange annual visual acuity testing by an optometrist from the time of school entry
options.rationale: Visual acuity is preserved until posterior synechiae, band keratopathy or cataract have already formed, so acuity testing detects the disease too late. The eye also needs magnified examination of the anterior chamber, which an acuity chart cannot provide. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis)
source_refs: Australian Rheumatology Association: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis

options.text: Arrange slit lamp examination now and then repeat it every twelve months
options.rationale: Twelve monthly screening is the interval used for the lowest risk groups, such as older children with rheumatoid factor positive polyarticular disease or systemic onset disease. Applying it to a young antinuclear antibody positive girl leaves a year in which silent inflammation can scar the anterior chamber. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis)
source_refs: Australian Rheumatology Association: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis

options.text: Arrange fundoscopy at each rheumatology visit and refer her if it looks abnormal
options.rationale: Fundoscopy examines the posterior segment, whereas this disease inflames the anterior chamber, where cells and flare are only visible on slit lamp examination. A normal fundus therefore provides false reassurance. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis)
source_refs: Australian Rheumatology Association: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis

options.text: Arrange slit lamp examination now and then repeat it every three months
options.rationale: Onset under 7 years with oligoarticular disease and a positive antinuclear antibody defines the highest risk group for chronic anterior uveitis, and three monthly slit lamp screening is the recommended interval for the first several years. Screening continues on this schedule even when the arthritis is in remission, because eye and joint activity are not correlated. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis)
source_refs: Australian Rheumatology Association: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis

explanation.summary: Chronic anterior uveitis complicates up to a fifth of oligoarticular juvenile idiopathic arthritis and is the main cause of preventable visual loss in this population. Risk is stratified by three variables: subtype, age at onset and antinuclear antibody status, with young antinuclear antibody positive girls with oligoarticular disease at the top of the risk table and screened three monthly. The inflammation is silent, so the child gives no warning and the first sign may be an irregular pupil from posterior synechiae or a reduced red reflex from cataract. Screening intervals lengthen with time since diagnosis and with increasing age, but surveillance continues for years and is not stopped when the joints settle. Established uveitis is treated with topical corticosteroid and mydriatics, escalating to methotrexate and then adalimumab if control is not achieved.
key_points: Risk stratification uses subtype, age at onset and antinuclear antibody status
Antinuclear antibody positive oligoarticular disease with onset under 7 years is screened three monthly
The uveitis is asymptomatic, so symptom-triggered review is unsafe
Slit lamp examination is required; acuity testing and fundoscopy both miss it
Eye and joint disease activity are independent, so screening continues in joint remission
explanation.pearls: Adalimumab combined with methotrexate outperforms methotrexate alone for refractory juvenile idiopathic arthritis associated uveitis; etanercept is the anti-tumour necrosis factor agent that does not work for the eye disease despite controlling the joints.

sources.label: Australian Rheumatology Association: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis
BMJ Best Practice: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis

subtopic_detail: Urgency of referral for a unilateral white pupillary reflex noticed on family photographs
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 14-month-old girl whose father shows you four photographs taken over the past two months. In each one her right pupil looks white while the left shows the usual red glow of a camera flash.

Her mother adds that over the last three weeks the right eye 'drifts in towards her nose' when she is tired, and that she seems to bump into things on that side. The girl was born at term, has no relevant family history and her development is on track.

On examination visual behaviour is asymmetric: she objects when you occlude the left eye but not when you occlude the right. The right red reflex is dull and pale compared with a bright red reflex on the left. The cornea is clear and the eye is white and not watering, and there is no proptosis. Cover testing reveals an inward shift of the right eye.

data_table.Ocular examination: Right red reflex dull and pale, left bright red; cornea clear, conjunctiva white, no watering, no proptosis
data_table.Visual behaviour: Objects to occlusion of the left eye but not the right
data_table.Cover test: Inward shift of the right eye on cover testing

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer to paediatric ophthalmology for examination under anaesthesia within this week
options.rationale: An asymmetric white reflex with a new squint in a toddler demands dilated fundus examination under anaesthesia at a tertiary centre within days, because retinoblastoma is the diagnosis that must be excluded first and survival and eye salvage both fall sharply with delay. Squint developing in the second year is a recognised second presentation of the same disease once central vision has been lost. (Source: RCH CPG: Red reflex and leukocoria)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Red reflex and leukocoria

options.text: Refer to orthoptics for a squint assessment at the next available clinic appointment
options.rationale: Treating this as an isolated squint ignores the abnormal red reflex, which is the finding that changes the differential entirely. Routine orthoptic referral would be right for a comitant squint with symmetrical bright red reflexes and normal visual behaviour. (Source: RCH CPG: Red reflex and leukocoria)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Red reflex and leukocoria

options.text: Arrange an outpatient orbital ultrasound and review her with the result in a month
options.rationale: Ultrasound can demonstrate an intraocular mass with calcification but it neither excludes small tumours nor stages the eye, and a month of waiting is unacceptable. Imaging is arranged by the ophthalmology service alongside examination under anaesthesia, not instead of it. (Source: RCH CPG: Red reflex and leukocoria)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Red reflex and leukocoria

options.text: Reassure the parents that the appearance is a camera flash artefact and review as needed
options.rationale: A pseudoleukocoria from off-axis flash is symmetrical or varies between photographs, whereas this is reproducibly unilateral across four images and is confirmed by a dull red reflex on examination. Reassurance in this setting is the commonest route to a delayed diagnosis. (Source: RCH CPG: Red reflex and leukocoria)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Red reflex and leukocoria

options.text: Prescribe patching of the left eye and refer to ophthalmology within the next three months
options.rationale: Occlusion therapy treats amblyopia once a structural cause of reduced vision has been excluded, and patching the better eye here would leave a child functionally blind while a tumour goes untreated. Amblyopia therapy follows the fundus examination, never precedes it. (Source: RCH CPG: Red reflex and leukocoria)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Red reflex and leukocoria

explanation.summary: Leukocoria is an abnormal white pupillary reflex and is the presenting sign in roughly 60 per cent of retinoblastomas, with squint accounting for a further 20 per cent. Other causes include congenital cataract, persistent foetal vasculature, Coats disease, toxocariasis and retinopathy of prematurity, and all of them warrant prompt ophthalmological assessment because visual development is time critical. Parents commonly notice the abnormality in photographs before any clinician does, and a parental report of a white reflex should be believed even if the reflex looks normal in a brightly lit consulting room. Examination under anaesthesia with full mydriasis and scleral indentation is the definitive assessment, since a struggling toddler cannot be adequately examined awake. Retinoblastoma is heritable in about 40 per cent of cases, so genetic counselling and examination of siblings follow the diagnosis.
key_points: Compare the red reflexes of both eyes in the same view; asymmetry is the abnormal finding
Leukocoria and new squint are the two commonest presentations of retinoblastoma
Believe a parental report of a white reflex in photographs even if your examination looks normal
Definitive assessment is dilated examination under anaesthesia at a tertiary centre within days
Never patch an eye for presumed amblyopia before a structural cause has been excluded
explanation.pearls: Around 40 per cent of retinoblastoma is heritable through a germline RB1 mutation, and those children need lifelong surveillance for second primary cancers, particularly osteosarcoma, which is why genetic testing is arranged at diagnosis rather than later.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Red reflex and leukocoria

subtopic_detail: Score threshold for starting pharmacological treatment of neonatal abstinence and the feeding decision
stem:
You are the resident on the postnatal ward caring for a 4-day-old boy born at 38 weeks to a mother who has been on supervised methadone 60 mg daily for two years through an opioid treatment program. Urine drug screening at booking and at delivery detected methadone only.

He was born by normal vaginal delivery weighing 2900 g. He is rooming in with his mother in a quiet, dimly lit single room, is being swaddled and held skin to skin, and is breastfeeding every two to three hours.

Over the last twelve hours the midwife has recorded modified Finnegan scores of 9, 10 and 9 on three consecutive four hourly assessments. He is tremulous when disturbed, has a high pitched cry that settles with holding, sleeps less than an hour after feeds and has had three loose stools. Glucose, electrolytes and temperature are all within normal limits and there are no seizures.

data_table.Scores: Modified Finnegan scores 9, 10 and 9 on three consecutive four hourly assessments
data_table.Clinical features: Tremor on handling, high pitched cry settling with holding, sleep less than one hour after feeds, three loose stools
data_table.Investigations: Blood glucose, electrolytes and temperature within normal limits; no seizure activity
data_table.Care to date: Rooming in, quiet dim environment, swaddling, skin to skin, breastfeeding two to three hourly

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence oral phenobarbitone, continue rooming in and support continued breastfeeding
options.rationale: Phenobarbitone is the agent of choice when the withdrawal is from a non-opioid sedative or when polysubstance exposure is documented, and it is added as a second agent if morphine alone fails. Using it first for pure methadone withdrawal treats the wrong receptor and brings unnecessary sedation. (Source: NSW Health: Neonatal abstinence syndrome)
source_refs: NSW Health: Neonatal abstinence syndrome

options.text: Commence oral morphine, continue rooming in and support continued breastfeeding
options.rationale: Three consecutive modified Finnegan scores of 8 or more is the trigger for pharmacological treatment, and oral morphine is first line for opioid withdrawal because it replaces the same receptor activity and is weaned predictably. Breastfeeding continues because methadone transfers into milk in very small quantities and reduces both the severity and duration of withdrawal. (Source: NSW Health: Neonatal abstinence syndrome)
source_refs: NSW Health: Neonatal abstinence syndrome

options.text: Continue non-pharmacological care alone and rescore him on four hourly cycles
options.rationale: Optimised non-pharmacological care is the foundation of management and is already in place, but it has not held the scores below threshold across three consecutive assessments. Persisting with it alone risks poor feeding, weight loss and seizures. (Source: NSW Health: Neonatal abstinence syndrome)
source_refs: NSW Health: Neonatal abstinence syndrome

options.text: Commence oral clonidine, continue rooming in and support continued breastfeeding
options.rationale: Clonidine is an adjunct used to reduce total opioid exposure or when morphine weaning stalls, not a first-line single agent. Its hypotensive and bradycardic effects also require closer monitoring than a postnatal ward usually provides. (Source: NSW Health: Neonatal abstinence syndrome)
source_refs: NSW Health: Neonatal abstinence syndrome

options.text: Advise formula feeding, transfer him to the nursery and commence oral morphine
options.rationale: Separating mother and baby worsens withdrawal scores and removes the single most effective non-pharmacological intervention, and stopping breastfeeding removes the small protective opioid transfer through milk. Formula feeding is advised for maternal human immunodeficiency virus infection or ongoing unsanctioned drug use, neither of which applies here. (Source: NSW Health: Neonatal abstinence syndrome)
source_refs: NSW Health: Neonatal abstinence syndrome

explanation.summary: Neonatal abstinence syndrome follows in utero exposure to opioids and presents with central nervous system irritability, autonomic overactivity and gastrointestinal dysfunction, typically within 24 to 72 hours for heroin and later, up to 5 to 7 days, for methadone because of its longer half-life. Scoring systems such as the modified Finnegan tool exist to make the decision to treat reproducible rather than impressionistic, and the standard triggers are three consecutive scores of 8 or more or two consecutive scores of 12 or more. Non-pharmacological care, meaning rooming in, minimal handling, a quiet dim environment, swaddling and frequent small feeds, reduces the proportion of babies who need drug treatment and is never abandoned when medication starts. Oral morphine is first line for opioid withdrawal, weaned by protocol once scores have been controlled for 24 to 48 hours. Breastfeeding is actively encouraged for mothers stable on methadone or buprenorphine, and babies exposed to methadone need observation for at least 5 days before discharge.
key_points: Treat when three consecutive modified Finnegan scores are 8 or more, or two are 12 or more
Oral morphine is first line for opioid withdrawal; phenobarbitone is for sedative or polysubstance exposure
Non-pharmacological care continues alongside drug treatment, it is not replaced by it
Breastfeeding is encouraged on stable methadone or buprenorphine and shortens withdrawal
Methadone exposed babies are observed for at least 5 days because onset is delayed
explanation.pearls: Naloxone is contraindicated at the birth of an opioid exposed baby even when the baby is apnoeic, because it precipitates acute withdrawal and seizures; ventilate instead and let the exposure wear off.

subtopic_detail: Imaging and drainage decision in parapneumonic collection failing 48 hours of intravenous antibiotics
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 4-year-old girl who was admitted 48 hours ago with right sided pneumonia and started on intravenous benzylpenicillin. Her mother says she is 'no better at all' and is still hot and breathing fast.

She remains febrile to 39.2°C with ongoing tachypnoea and now lies curled towards her right side and cries when moved. Her oxygen requirement has risen from room air to 2 L/min by nasal prongs to keep saturations at 94 per cent.

On examination there is stony dullness to percussion over the right lower zone with absent breath sounds and reduced chest wall movement on that side. A repeat chest radiograph shows opacification of the right hemithorax to the level of the hilum with a meniscus. Blood cultures taken on admission remain negative and inflammatory markers have risen.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 148/min, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 44/min, SpO2 94 per cent on 2 L/min nasal prongs, temperature 39.2°C
data_table.Examination: Stony dullness and absent breath sounds over the right lower zone with reduced chest wall movement
data_table.Imaging: Chest radiograph shows right hemithorax opacification to hilar level with a meniscus
data_table.Investigations: C-reactive protein 218 mg/L (less than 5), white cell count 24.6 x10^9/L (4.0-12.0), blood cultures negative at 48 hours

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue the intravenous antibiotics for a further 48 hours and repeat the chest film
options.rationale: Persistent fever, rising inflammatory markers and a rising oxygen requirement at 48 hours define antibiotic failure, and a loculated collection will not resolve with more of the same therapy. Continued observation alone is reasonable only for a small free-flowing effusion in a child who is improving. (Source: RCH CPG: Pneumonia)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Pneumonia

options.text: Arrange contrast computed tomography of the chest and refer her to cardiothoracic surgery
options.rationale: Computed tomography adds radiation without changing the initial drainage decision and is reserved for suspected necrotising pneumonia, bronchopleural fistula or failure of chest drainage. Ultrasound answers the question of loculation better and with no ionising radiation. (Source: RCH CPG: Pneumonia)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Pneumonia

options.text: Perform a diagnostic pleural tap and discharge her home on oral antibiotics afterwards
options.rationale: A diagnostic tap without a drain leaves the collection in place, and a child on supplemental oxygen with a rising C-reactive protein is not dischargeable. Simple aspiration alone is an option only for a small, free-flowing, non-purulent effusion. (Source: RCH CPG: Pneumonia)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Pneumonia

options.text: Arrange chest ultrasound then insert a chest drain with an intrapleural fibrinolytic agent
options.rationale: Ultrasound is the imaging of choice to size the collection and demonstrate septations, and a large loculated empyema in a child failing antibiotics is drained with a small bore catheter plus intrapleural urokinase or alteplase. This combination shortens hospital stay and has outcomes equivalent to primary video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery at lower cost. (Source: RCH CPG: Pneumonia)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Pneumonia

options.text: Change to intravenous vancomycin and meropenem and repeat the blood cultures every day
options.rationale: Broadening antibiotic cover does not address the mechanical problem of a loculated collection that antibiotics penetrate poorly, though cover is usually widened to include Staphylococcus aureus at the time of drainage. Blood cultures are positive in only a minority of paediatric empyema and repeating them daily will not guide management. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic

explanation.summary: A parapneumonic effusion complicates a significant minority of childhood bacterial pneumonias and progresses through an exudative phase, a fibrinopurulent phase with septation, and finally an organising phase with a fibrous peel. The decision point is not the presence of fluid but whether the child is failing treatment, judged by persistent fever beyond 48 hours, rising inflammatory markers, an increasing oxygen requirement or a rising respiratory rate. Ultrasound is the first imaging test because it distinguishes free fluid from septated collections, estimates volume and marks a safe drainage site, all without radiation. Small bore pigtail drainage with intrapleural fibrinolysis is the standard first intervention in Australian paediatric centres, with video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery reserved for failure. Streptococcus pneumoniae remains the commonest organism but Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus pyogenes are over-represented in empyema, so antibiotic cover is broadened at the time of drainage.
key_points: Failure at 48 hours means persistent fever, rising markers or a rising oxygen requirement
Ultrasound is the imaging of choice; computed tomography is reserved for complications
Small bore drain plus intrapleural fibrinolytic is the standard first intervention
Broadening antibiotics alone does not treat a loculated collection
Cover Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus pyogenes once empyema is confirmed
explanation.pearls: Long-term lung function after paediatric empyema is essentially normal even when the radiograph remains abnormal for months, so persistent opacification at discharge is not a reason to extend antibiotics or re-drain.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Parapneumonic effusion and empyema
